blogs.title: When ‘Substantial Evidence’ Isn’t: The Federal Circuit’s Hard Look at Self-Contradictory Expert Testimony
blogs.description: The court reversed JMOL denials on both patents largely because Finesse’s expert could not consistently map claim elements to the accused Nokia radios. Focusing on the ’134 patent, the panel treated the expert’s pivot—from identifying the modeled PIM path as the “interference generating signals” to vaguely invoking x1/x2—as the kind of incoherence that cannot sustain a verdict under the substantial-evidence standard. The post explores how the Fifth Circuit’s JMOL lens interacts with Federal Circuit patent sufficiency review, why Johns Hopkins v. Datascope gives teeth to policing contradictory testimony, and practical lessons for ensuring clean, unequivocal element-by-element mappings at trial.

blogs.title: ‘Three Signals’ Means Separately Identifiable, Not Unique: Claim Construction, Prosecution History, and Avoiding Disavowal
blogs.description: On the ’775 patent, the panel rejected AT&T/Nokia’s argument that “S1, S2, and S3” must be unique, holding there was no clear and unambiguous disavowal during prosecution when Finesse amended from “two or three signals” to “three signals.” The court endorsed a construction requiring three separately identifiable signals, not necessarily three unique ones. This post unpacks the intrinsic/extrinsic path the district court and Federal Circuit followed, the limits of prosecution-history-based narrowing, and drafting/litigation takeaways for practitioners arguing about signal identity vs. separability in digital-signal-processing claims.

blogs.title: Seven Means Seven: Algebraic Specificity and the Perils of Post-Hoc Mapping in DSP Patent Cases
blogs.description: The ’775 patent fell on proof, not claim scope: Finesse offered only three distinct multiplications from Nokia’s documentation to meet a claim that requires seven third-order products of S1, S2, and S3. The evidence involved modulus and complex conjugates, not the claimed products, and the expert never provided a concrete mapping. This post examines why mathematical exactitude matters in software/DSP infringement cases, how demonstratives must align with claimed operations, and why appellate courts will reject attempts to retrofit a compliant mapping for the first time on appeal.

blogs.title: From Liability to a Vacated $166 Million Award: Damages as a Passenger on JMOL Reversals—and Trial Preservation Lessons
blogs.description: Because the court reversed on noninfringement for both patents, it vacated the lump-sum damages award. This post surveys the strategic implications for damages presentation in EDTX and elsewhere when liability is fragile, the importance of preserving Rule 50(a) issues (including the district court’s waiver ruling that the Federal Circuit bypassed in part), and practical tips: align damages models with specific, well-supported infringement theories; build records that survive appellate scrutiny; and be wary of all-or-nothing verdict forms when infringement hinges on technical minutiae.
